d.title: Two methods, two implementations, and neither is production
d.caption: **Read the names carefully, because both shipped services are development conveniences.** The in-memory one is lost on restart and not shared between replicas, so every deploy prompts the user to authorise again. The session-state one puts the token in the dictionary that gets interpolated into instructions and read by every tool and callback. **A long-lived refresh token belongs in a secrets manager behind a service you implement** — which is two methods of work.

d.title: Five places a secret must not go, and what reaches each one
d.caption: **The rule is not “do not show the secret to the user” — it is “do not put the secret anywhere the model can read”**, because a sufficiently determined user will get the model to repeat its instruction, and a tool result is in the transcript the model is already reading. **The fourth row is the one that surprises people:** the agent object is shared across concurrent invocations, so a token stashed on `self` becomes everyone's token. Tools should hold credentials in their own closure or fetch them at call time, and return data, never keys.

d.title: Four tenancy boundaries, and only one of them is real
d.caption: **`app_name` is part of the storage key, so two apps do not see each other's sessions — but it is configuration, not something you can vary per request**, which makes it a product separator rather than a security boundary. The `app:` row is the most common state-scope mistake with a security consequence. **Enforcement belongs in the database**, as row-level security or an unavoidable predicate keyed by the authenticated principal: if the only thing separating tenants is a WHERE clause the model influences, they are not separated.

d.title: The attacker's sentence arrived with role=user
d.caption: **Not a special “tool data” role, not quoted, not escaped — the same role your actual user's messages use.** The system instruction still said “never issue refunds”, and whether the model honours that over the sentence inside the ticket depends entirely on the model's training: a probability, not a guarantee. **Everything in this lesson follows from accepting that.** You cannot make the text safe, so you make the consequences safe.

d.title: Policy the model cannot argue with - and the log line that proves it fires
d.caption: **The callback compares the requested account against the caller's and refuses, which is not negotiable in the way an instruction is.** Returning a structured error means the model relays a sentence the user can act on and does not retry — raising ends the turn in a stack trace and teaches it nothing. **The log line is half the value:** a blocked call is a signal that something tried, and “how often does this fire” is a question you want answerable on day one rather than after an incident.

d.title: Naming text untrusted raises the bar; it does not build a wall
d.caption: **Marking provenance measurably helps and costs almost nothing** — the model gets an explicit cue that this field is data to summarise rather than instructions to follow. **What it cannot do is make your instruction privileged**, because both are still text in one prompt with the same role. Treat it as one layer among several, and never as the reason a dangerous tool is safe to expose: the mitigation is the note, the boundary is the narrow tool and the scoped credential.

d.title: Four output checks, and what each one costs per turn
d.caption: **The secret-scan row is worth reading twice: it should never fire, and when it does you have found a real bug upstream** rather than a model quirk. **And the arithmetic at the bottom is the decision.** A model-based input classifier plus a model-based output check is two extra round trips on every single turn — defensible for an agent that can move money, indefensible for one that answers questions about opening hours. The structural defences cost nothing per turn and should be there regardless.

d.title: One flag, and the callable form that makes it a rule
d.caption: **`require_confirmation=True` sits at the agent definition where a reviewer can see it, and cannot be forgotten inside a branch** — which is exactly what you want for the rule itself. **The callable form is the one to reach for in practice:** approval that depends on the arguments, so a refund of four pounds goes straight through and one of four hundred stops. A flag that stops everything produces approval fatigue, which section 04 names as worse than no approval at all.

d.title: Five things happened, and the first is that the body never ran
d.caption: **The pause is durable because it is an event, not a coroutine waiting in memory** — so it survives a deploy, a crash, and a load balancer sending the next request to a different replica. That is the difference between an approval mechanism you can run in production and one that works on a laptop. **Note the error returned for the real tool:** the model is told the action did not happen, so it says approval was requested rather than claiming the refund went through.

d.title: Six things ADK does not do for you
d.caption: **ADK gives you a durable pause and a record of what was proposed; everything in this table is yours.** The first row is the one with teeth: nothing checks who approves, so your interface authorises the reviewer — and the reviewer must not be the person who asked. **And the last line of the lesson is the one to act on:** if approvals are frequent the threshold is wrong. A person clicking through forty near-identical requests is a rubber stamp with a name attached, and an approval step that is always approved is worse than none because it manufactures the appearance of oversight.

d.title: The flag for the rule, the manual call for the message
d.caption: **Many production tools use both, and for different reasons.** The flag is enforcement: declarative, visible, impossible to forget inside a branch. The manual `request_confirmation` earns its place when the human needs context the arguments do not carry — the customer's history, the three previous refunds this month, why the agent thinks this one is justified. **And note the state machine in the manual form:** no confirmation yet means ask and return; a confirmation that is not confirmed means declined, with `retryable: False` so the model stops asking.
